original_content.knowledge_point: Determining a Valid Region to Define a Double Integral Over a Non-Rectangular Domain
original_content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14053940/assets/9d4a0a08513d817fe841f1e45e5d363d6e64241837dea71f38aef452f86b08a7.png)

Consider the region $D$ shown above. If 

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,{∬}_{D}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

which of the following could be the definition of the rectangular domain $R?$

- $R=[0,1]\times [-1,1]$
- $R=[0,2]\times [-1,1]$
- $R=[0,2]\times [0,1]$
original_content.worked_solution:
Notice that if $R$ covers $D$ completely and we define 

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D,\end{aligned}
$$

we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given rectangles.

- Rectangles I and III do not cover the region $D.$

- Rectangle II covers the region $D$ completely.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

- $R=[0,2]\times [0,1]$
corrected_content.worked_solution:
The displayed region includes points with $x>1$, so rectangle I, $[0,1]\times[-1,1]$, does not contain all of $D$. It includes points with $y<0$, so rectangle III, $[0,2]\times[0,1]$, also fails the containment requirement. The entire drawn region lies in rectangle II, $[0,2]\times[-1,1]$.

The region lies strictly to the right of the $y$-axis, so $3y^2/x$ is defined throughout $D$. For rectangle II, $f$ equals this integrand on $D$ and zero outside $D$ in $R$; in particular its zero branch applies on $x=0$, which is outside $D$. Hence $\iint_R f\,dA=\iint_D3y^2/x\,dA$. The correct answer is "II only".
